title: Repository automation · Controlling execution
description: Design an unattended workflow with a clear trigger, task contract, permissions, evidence and approval boundary. Use execution controls to limit cost and blast radius without mistaking them for proof of correctness.

blocks.body:
The team has a useful investigator. Given a failed retry-test run, it can inspect the log, find the relevant source and prepare a diagnosis for review. An engineer has been starting it manually. Now the team wants it to run when the check fails.

That adds a new problem before the investigation even begins. A repository emits many events: a push, a queued check, a completed check, a rerun and perhaps several notifications about the same underlying failure. Which one is the request to do work?

Suppose we select completed failures of the named retry check. The workflow records the repository, check-run identity and tested revision. It then creates an investigation with that evidence. A rerun of the check may deserve a fresh observation; a repeated delivery of the same notification usually should not create a second independent investigation.

Those are decisions for the outer workflow. The model can help interpret a failure once invoked, but it does not supply reliable event identity merely by remembering that it has seen a similar log. Keep the identity and execution status in durable state the workflow can inspect.

The revision also needs care. A failure notification refers to code that ran at a particular point. Checking out the branch's latest state may investigate a different program. Start with the tested revision or explicitly record why you are examining a later one. Otherwise, the investigator can produce a convincing explanation of code that never caused the reported failure.

A schedule has the same obligations. 'Every night' specifies when to look; it does not specify which failures are new, which already have an investigation, or what counts as a useful result. Write those rules before allowing a recurring job to accumulate reports.

sections.title: Follow the report all the way out

blocks.body:
**Worked Example**

A repository wants a nightly dependency advisory report. The job reads the dependency manifest and lockfile at a recorded revision, runs the advisory check and gathers evidence for anything that needs attention. It should leave maintainers a reviewable finding rather than update versions on its own.

There are two distinct operations in that description. Investigating requires access to dependency information and the advisory source. Publishing requires permission to write to the chosen destination. The investigator can produce an artifact containing a proposed report without holding the account permissions that publish it.

That separation is useful even when both stages are automated. The publishing stage can check that the output has the expected repository identity, evidence links and permitted destination. It can reject an oversized or malformed result. It can also determine whether a report for the same advisory and dependency state already exists. These checks constrain the operation; they do not establish that every sentence of the diagnosis is correct.

A human review may still be appropriate for the interpretation or proposed remedy. Decide whether it happens before publication or after a clearly labelled draft is created. A draft issue or pull request is itself an external write, even though it is not a merge or release. Give that write an explicit policy.

GitHub Agentic Workflows provides a concrete implementation to examine. Its documented Safe Outputs architecture separates the agent job from jobs that perform scoped external writes. Read the [permission-isolation diagram](https://github.github.com/gh-aw/introduction/architecture/#safe-outputs-permission-isolation) and follow the output artifact between them. Compare where the permissions are held with the two operations in our advisory example. Use the documentation for your installed version when implementing the configuration.

The pattern remains useful beyond that product. An investigator proposes an effect, and another component validates and performs the allowed operation. If the investigator still has a broad token that can bypass this path, the separation exists only in the diagram.

Most recurring jobs should sometimes have nothing to report. If the dependency state and relevant advisories have not changed, another public issue adds work for the maintainer. A recorded no-action outcome can be the correct result.

But 'nothing actionable found' and 'could not query the advisory service' are different outcomes. The first requires a completed investigation adequate for that conclusion. The second is a failure to obtain evidence. Treating both as an empty report makes an outage look like reassuring news.

Keep a small durable account of the run: what it examined, how it ended, and where its evidence or failure details can be found. Notify the responsible person when action is needed, using a policy that avoids repeatedly announcing the same known problem. A job that never started will not produce its own failure report, so observation of the schedule belongs outside the job itself.

Also provide a way to disable the recurring trigger without depending on the agent to repair itself. Once disabled, inspect any active executions separately; stopping future triggers does not necessarily cancel work already underway.

These details matter to usefulness as much as to correctness. A maintainer who must read ten empty or duplicated reports to find one relevant finding has inherited a new triage queue.

blocks.question: The advisory service times out and the job creates no issue. Is that a successful no-action outcome?
blocks.answer: No. The job has not obtained the evidence needed to conclude that there is nothing to report. It should record the service failure and its recovery status, rather than present the absence of an issue as a completed investigation.

sections.title: What a limit can tell you

blocks.body:
Imagine one nightly run spends an hour trying variations of a failing test command. A duration limit would contain that cost. It would not tell us whether the cause was bad setup, a difficult diagnosis or an agent repeating an unhelpful action.

Set limits for the resources the job can consume: elapsed time, tool attempts, spend where enforceable, and overlapping executions. Choose them from the expected work and the consequences of an overrun. The numbers are operating decisions, not universal recommendations.

Each limit needs an owner and a response. A wall-clock deadline belongs in an executor or scheduler that can stop the actual work, including relevant subprocesses. A concurrency limit needs a defined scope: one job per repository, per revision or per incident may produce quite different behaviour. A retry allowance should distinguish a transient read failure from an uncertain write.

Reserve time to save the evidence and report partial progress where possible. Do not make recovery depend entirely on a graceful final model message; the process may be terminated before it can produce one. Persist important observations as work proceeds.

Keep the execution outcome alongside the task outcome. A run can stop within budget while returning an unsupported diagnosis. Another can hit its time limit after finding useful evidence but before completing the investigation. The first is not made correct by being cheap; the second need not lose the evidence it obtained.

Reaching a limit should prompt a decision about continuation, changed scope or a repair to the environment. Automatically starting another identical run with a fresh budget would evade the limit while retaining the underlying problem.

sections.title: The report was created, but the acknowledgement was lost

blocks.body:
The publishing stage sends its report. The destination creates the issue, but the network connection drops before the workflow receives the issue identifier. From the workflow's perspective, the request timed out.

Blindly repeating it can create a second issue. Simply marking it failed can leave a real published result unaccounted for. The correct next step is to reconcile the uncertain outcome with the destination.

Give the logical publication a stable identity. Where supported, an idempotency key lets retries refer to the same operation. Otherwise, retain a durable record and a destination marker that makes the original result discoverable. Reuse that identity after a timeout; generating a new one for every attempt defeats its purpose.

A marker lookup followed by creation can still race if two jobs do it simultaneously. Use an appropriate uniqueness guarantee, lock or destination-supported operation when the workflow needs to exclude that race. A concurrency setting is helpful only if its scope covers the competing writers.

You can learn a great deal with three small trials: deliver an event twice, run an investigation with no relevant change, and lose the acknowledgement after publication. Inspect both the workflow record and the destination. Does one logical investigation produce one intended result? Can an operator distinguish a quiet run from missing evidence and an uncertain publication?

The next chapter examines which of these responsibilities an existing harness or workflow already supplies, and when a small custom component is worth owning. The concrete failure you need to handle will be a better guide than the desire to build a platform.

heading: What happens when nobody is there to start the job?
lead: Follow a recurring investigation from event to report, including the quiet runs, duplicated deliveries and interruptions that determine whether it is useful to operate.
